findings.title: Missing `prisma` import causes ReferenceError / compile failure
findings.body: The new refresh-token logic added to `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update({...})` (around line 96-99), but the file never imports `prisma` (compare with other CalendarService files that do `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`). This will fail TypeScript compilation (no symbol `prisma` in scope) or throw a ReferenceError at runtime, breaking Salesforce OAuth token refresh entirely.

findings.title: Credential key saved as the whole safeParse result instead of the parsed token data
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full `z.SafeParseReturnType` object (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data itself (see packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts). Here the code does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then persists `data: { key }` directly to `prisma.credential.update`. This stores `{ success: true, data: {...} }` as the credential's `key` JSON instead of the actual token fields (access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, etc.), corrupting the stored Google Calendar credential and breaking any subsequent code that reads `credential.key.access_token` etc. Other call sites of this helper (office365, salesforce, zoom) correctly destructure `.data`; this one does not.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens return type mismatch breaks token refresh when credential sync is enabled
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` `Response` object when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` + `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, but the non-sync branch here returns `fetchTokens.res` (the googleapis client's internal response object which exposes `.data`). The caller unconditionally does `const token = res?.data;` then `token.access_token` — a bare `fetch` Response has no `.data` property, so when credential syncing is enabled this will throw a TypeError (`Cannot read properties of undefined`), breaking Google Calendar token refresh for any self-hoster who enables the very feature this PR introduces.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens result treated as a parsed HubspotToken when sync is enabled, but it is a raw fetch Response
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, but the normal path returns the already-parsed object from `hubspotClient.oauth.tokensApi.createToken(...)`. The code immediately treats the result as a `HubspotToken` (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`, `.accessToken`, `.tokenType`), which are undefined on a raw Response object. This produces `NaN` expiry dates and `undefined` access tokens being persisted to the DB and passed to `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` when the sync feature is enabled.

findings.title: Dynamic schema keys using `.toString()` do not do what the comments claim
findings.body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` tries to build dynamic keys with `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not return a property name derived from the response data; it returns the default `Object.prototype.toString` value (effectively the same literal string, e.g. `"[object Object]"`) for both expressions, and the second object-literal key overwrites the first. The net effect is that the "assume any numeric property is the expiry" validation described in the comment never happens — the schema ends up only requiring `access_token` with an unrelated optional unknown field under a bogus key name. This silently weakens validation of credential-sync responses without the dead code being obviously non-functional.

findings.title: Unhandled exceptions from zod `.parse()` and `symmetricDecrypt` return raw 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31) and `symmetricDecrypt(...)` (lines 57-59) are called without try/catch. A malformed request body or malformed/incorrectly-keyed ciphertext will throw an uncaught exception instead of a clean 400 response, resulting in an unhandled Next.js API error (500) and potentially leaking internal error details/stack traces to the caller. These should be wrapped and translated into controlled error responses (e.g. using `safeParse` and a try/catch around decryption).

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non constant-time string inequality
findings.body: The webhook secret validation uses a plain `!==` comparison between the incoming header and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that could help an attacker incrementally guess the secret. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) should be used for secret validation on an endpoint explicitly designed to create/update user credentials.

findings.title: redirect_uri hardcoded, now inconsistent with callback.ts which still uses appConfig.slug
findings.body: This PR changes `add.ts` to build the redirect URI with a hardcoded string `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` instead of `` `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback` ``, while `zoho-bigin/api/callback.ts` in this same PR still builds its redirect URI using `appConfig.slug`. If `appConfig.slug` ever changes, these two files will silently diverge and the OAuth redirect URI will stop matching between the authorize and callback steps, breaking the integration. This change also appears unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (credential syncing).

findings.title: No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or OAuth refresh changes
findings.body: The PR explicitly notes no tests were added, and this review found multiple concrete runtime bugs introduced by the OAuth refresh/credential-sync changes (e.g., response-shape mismatches in googlecalendar/hubspot CalendarService, a missing import in salesforce CalendarService, and a broken dynamic zod schema). None of the new files (`app-credential.ts`, `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`) nor the modified `CalendarService`/`VideoApiAdapter` refresh logic have unit or integration tests, so these regressions would not be caught by CI.
